Luke 15:10. There will be joy in the presence of the angels. If angels mutually rejoice with each other in heaven, when they see that what had wandered is restored to the fold, we too, who have the same cause in common with them, ought to be partakers of the same joy But. how does he say that the repentance of one ungodly man yields greater joy than the perseverance of many righteous men to angels, whose highest delight is in a continued and uninterrupted course of righteousness? I reply, though it would be more agreeable to the wishes of angels (as it is also more desirable) that men should always remain in perfect integrity, yet as in the deliverance of a sinner, who had been already devoted to destruction, and had been cut off as a rotten member from the body, the mercy of God shines more brightly, he attributes to angels, after the manner of men, a greater joy arising out of an unexpected good.
Over one repenting sinner. The word repentance is specially limited to the conversion of those who, having altogether turned aside from God, rise as it were from death to life; for otherwise the exercise of repentance ought to be uninterrupted throughout our whole life,
“Tant que nous sommes en ce monde;” — “as long as we are in this world.”
and no man is exempted from this necessity, since every one is reminded by his imperfections that he ought to aim at daily progress. But it is one thing, when a man, who has already entered upon the right course, though he stumble, or fall, or even go astray, endeavors to reach the goal; and another thing, when a man leaves a road which was entirely wrong, or only starts in the right course.
“Quand celuy qui estoit du tout esgare tourne bride pour commencer a bien faire;” — “when he who had altogether gone astray turns round to begin to do well.”
Those who have already begun to regulate their life by the standard of the divine law, do not need that kind of repentance which consists in beginning to lead a holy and pious life, though they must groan
“Combien qu’il soit tousiours necessaire de gemir;” — “though it be necessary for them always to groan.”
under the infirmities of the flesh, and labor to correct them.

11. And he said,
“Il dit aussi;” — “he said also.”
A certain man had two sons: 12. And the younger of them said to his father, Father, give me the portion of property which falls to me. And he divided between them the property. 13. And not many days afterwards,
“Et peu de iours apres;” — “and a few days after.”
the younger son, having gathered all together, set out on a journey to a distant country, and there wasted his property by living extravagantly. 14. But when he had spent all, a sore famine arose in that country; and he began to be in want. 15. And he went and entered into the service of one of the inhabitants of that country; and he sent him into his field to feed swine. 16. And he was desirous to fill his belly with the husks on which the swine were feeding: and no man gave to him.
“Et (ou, mais) personne ne luy donnoit;” — “and (or, but) nobody gave to him.”
17. And when he came to himself, he said, How many hirelings of my father have abundance of bread,
“Combien y-a-il de mercenaires en la maison de mon pere, qui ont force pain;” — “how may hirelings are there in my father’s house, who have plenty of bread.”
while I perish with hunger! 18. I will arise, and go to my father,
“Ie partiray d’icy, et m’en iray a mon pere;” — “I will depart hence, and will go away to my father.”
and will say to him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, 19. And am no longer worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hirelings. 20. And he arose, and came to his father. And while he was yet afar off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. 21. And the son said to him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, and am no longer worthy to be called thy son. 22. And the father said to his servants, Bring out the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet: 23. And bring the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us feast, and be merry: 24. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.
“Car mon fils que voyci estoit mort, et il est retourne a vie: il estoit perdu, mais il est retrouve;” — “for this is my son who was dead, and he is returned to life; he was lost, but he is found again.”
And they began to be merry.

There is also ingratitude in leaving the old man, <note n="524"> <div sID="gen100567" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Delaissant le bon vieil hemme de pere</foreign>;” — “leaving the good old man his father.”<div eID="gen100567" type="x-p"/> </note> and not only withholding the performance of the duties which be owed to him, but crippling and diminishing the wealth of his house. <note n="525"> <div sID="gen100568" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais aussi diminue le bien de la maison, et en emporte une bonne partie</foreign>;” — “but also diminishes the wealth of the house, and carries off a good part of it.”<div eID="gen100568" type="x-p"/> </note> This is at length followed by wasteful luxury and wicked extravagance, by which he squanders all that he had. <note n="526"> <div sID="gen100569" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Tout ce qu’il avoit eu du pere</foreign>;” — “all that he had got from his father.”<div eID="gen100569" type="x-p"/> </note> After so many offenses he deserved to find his father implacable. <note n="527"> <div sID="gen100570" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il avoit bien merite de trouver puis apres un pere rigoreux, et qui teint son coeur contre luy iusqu’au bout</foreign>;” — “he had well deserved to find afterwards a father who was severe, and who kept his heart shut against him to the end.”<div eID="gen100570" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen100566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100571" type="x-p"/>Under this image our Lord unquestionably depicts to us the boundless goodness and inestimable forbearance of God, that no crimes, however aggravated, may deter us from the hope of obtaining pardon, There would be some foundation for the analogy, if we were to say that this foolish and insolent youth resembles those persons who, enjoying at the hand of God a great abundance of good things, are moved by a blind and mad ambition to be separated from Him, that they may enjoy perfect freedom; as if it were not more desirable than all the kingdoms of the world to live under the fatherly care and government of God. But as I am afraid that this allusion may be thought overstrained, I shall satisfy myself with the literal meaning; not that I disapprove of the opinion, that under this figure is reproved the madness of those who imagine that it will be advantageous for them to have something of their own, and to be rich apart from the heavenly Father; but that I now confine myself within the limits of a Commentator. <note n="528"> <div sID="gen100572" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pource que ie me tien maintenant dans mes limites, et ne veux point passer l’office d’expositeur</foreign>;” — “because I now keep myself within my limits, and do not wish to go beyond the duty of an expositor.”<div eID="gen100572" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen100571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100573" type="x-p"/>Christ here describes what usually happens with young men, when they are carried away by their natural disposition. Destitute of sound judgment, and maddened by passion, they are ill fitted for governing themselves, and are not restrained by fear or shame. It is therefore impossible but that they shall abandon themselves to every thing to which their sinful inclination prompts them, and rush on in a disgraceful course, till they are involved in shameful poverty. He afterwards describes the punishment which, in the righteous judgment of God, generally overtakes spendthrifts and prodigals. After having wickedly squandered their means, they are left to pine in hunger, and not having known how to use in moderation an abundant supply of the best bread, they are reduced to eat acorns and <hi type="italic">husks</hi>. In short, they become the companions of <hi type="italic">swine</hi>, and are made to feel that they are unworthy to partake of human food; for it is swinish gluttony <note n="529"> <div sID="gen100574" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">C’est une gourmandise plustost convenable a des porceaux qu’a des hommes</foreign>;” — “it is a gluttony more suitable to swine than to men.”<div eID="gen100574" type="x-p"/> </note> to squander wickedly what was given for the support of life. <note n="530"> <div sID="gen100575" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour subvenir aux necessitez de ceste vie</foreign>;” — “to supply the necessities of this life.”<div eID="gen100575" type="x-p"/> </note> As to the ingenious exposition which some have brought forward, that it is the just punishment of wicked scorn, when those who have rejected delicious bread in the house of our heavenly Father are driven by hunger to eat <hi type="italic">husks</hi>, it is a true and useful doctrine; but in the meantime, we must bear in mind the difference that exists between allegories and the natural meaning. <note n="531"> <div sID="gen100576" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais cependant il faut tousiours aviser quelle difference il y a entre les allegories et le vray sens naturel d’un passage</foreign>;” — “but yet we must always consider what difference there is between allegories and the true natural meaning of a passage.”<div eID="gen100576" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen100573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100577" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And was desirous to fill his belly.</hi> This means that, in consequence of hunger, he no longer thought of his former luxuries, but greedily devoured <hi type="italic">husks; </hi>for of that kind of food he could not be in want, when he was giving it to the <hi type="italic">swine</hi> There is a well-known saying of Cyrus who, having for a long time suffered hunger during a flight, and having been slightly refreshed by eating coarse black bread, declared that he had never tasted savory bread till now; so the young man who is here mentioned was compelled by necessity to betake himself with appetite to <hi type="italic">husks</hi> The reason is added, <hi type="italic">because no man gave to him;</hi> for the copulative conjunction <hi type="italic">and </hi>(<foreign xml:lang="el">καὶ</foreign>) must, in my opinion, signify <hi type="italic">because</hi>, <note n="532"> <div sID="gen100578" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Car selon mon avis ce mot et se doit resoudre en Car, ou Pource que</foreign>;” — “for in my opinion this word <hi type="italic">and</hi> must mean <hi type="italic">For</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Because</hi>.<hi type="italic">”</hi><div eID="gen100578" type="x-p"/> </note> and what is here said does not refer to <hi type="italic">husks</hi>, which he had at hand, but I understand the meaning to be, that no man pitied his poverty; for prodigals who throw away the whole of their property are persons whom no man thinks himself bound to relieve, — nay more, as they have been accustomed to squander every thing, men think that nothing ought to be given to them. <note n="533"> <div sID="gen100579" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il semble que ce qu’on leur donne soit autant de perdu</foreign>;” — “what is given to them appears to be as good as thrown away.”<div eID="gen100579" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen100577" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100565" osisID="Luke.15.12" type="section"/>

entries.content_plain: 20. And while he was still afar off. This is the main point of the parable. If men, who are by nature prone to revenge, and too tenacious of their own rights, are moved by fatherly love kindly to forgive their children, and freely to bring them back, when they are sunk in wretchedness, God, whose boundless goodness exceeds all the affection of parents, “ L’amour de tous les peres de ce monde ;” — “the love of all the fathers in the world.” will not treat us more harshly. “ Sera bien pour le moins aussi debonnaire envers nous ;” — “will be at least as gentle towards us.” And certainly nothing is here attributed to an earthly father which God does not promise with respect to himself. entries.content_osis: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.15.28" sID="gen100610" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28. </hi><hi type="italic">Therefore his father went out.</hi> By these words he reproaches hypocrites with intolerable pride, which makes it necessary that the Father should entreat them not to envy the compassion manifested to their brethren. Now though God does not entreat, yet by his example he exhorts us to bear with the faults of our brethren. And in order to take away every excuse from wicked severity, he not only introduces hypocrites as speaking, whose false boasting might be confuted, but even affirms that, though any man had discharged, in the most perfect manner, all the duties of piety towards the Father, yet he has no just reason to complain because his brother obtains pardon. It is certain, indeed, that the sincere worshippers of God are always pure and free from this malignant disposition; but the design of Christ is, to show that it would be unjust in any man to murmur on account of his brother having been received into favor, even though he were not inferior in holiness to the angels.<div eID="gen100611" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100610" osisID="Luke.15.28" type="section"/>

31. Son,
“Mon enfant;” — “my child.”
thou art always with me. This answer consists of two parts. The first is, that the first-born son has no reason to be angry, when he sees his brother kindly received without any loss to himself;
“Veu qu’il n’y perd rien;” — “since he loses nothing by it.”
and the second is, that, without paying any regard to his brother’s safety, he is grieved on account of the rejoicing occasioned by his return. All my property, says he, is thine: that is, “Though thou hast hitherto carried nothing away out of my house, it has been no loss to the for all is reserved for thee undiminished.”
“Ta condition n’en est pas pire; car ie te garde tousiours ton droict entier;” — “thy condition is not the worse for it; for I always preserve thy rights entire.”

if God graciously receives into favor those who had been at variance with him on account of their sins; and, on the other hand, it is wicked hardness of heart not to rejoice, when we see our brethren returned from death to life.
